title: Run Apache Spark and Iceberg 4.5x faster than open source Spark with Amazon EMR
key_points: Read-side companion to the write benchmark: AWS reports runs of 3 TB TPC-DS queries on Iceberg tables, EMR 7.12 runtime versus open-source Spark and Iceberg on equal EC2 clusters.
Credits metadata caching, parallel I/O, adaptive planning and fixes to Iceberg scan regressions, bringing Iceberg reads close to plain Parquet.
AWS reports up to 4.5x faster; mainly an argument for managed runtimes over self-run Spark.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg
decision: Managed EMR/Glue Spark runtime vs self-managed open-source Spark for Iceberg query workloads
authors: Atul Payapilly, Akshaya KP, Giovanni Matteo Fumarola, Hari Kishore Chaparala

title: Run Apache Spark and Apache Iceberg write jobs 2x faster with Amazon EMR
key_points: Benchmarks merge-heavy Iceberg writes (inserts, updates, deletes) on the EMR 7.12 Spark runtime against open-source Spark with Iceberg; AWS reports using 3 TB TPC-DS tables.
Gains come from metadata-only partition deletes, Bloom-filter joins inside MERGE and more parallel file writes; Glue uses the same optimised runtime.
AWS reports just over 2x faster, with an estimated run cost of about USD 1.58 versus 2.68; includes steps to reproduce the benchmark.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache Spark, Apache Iceberg
decision: Managed EMR/Glue Spark runtime vs self-managed open-source Spark for Iceberg MERGE workloads
authors: Atul Payapilly, Akshaya KP, Giovanni Matteo Fumarola, Hari Kishore Chaparala

title: Medidata’s journey to a modern lakehouse architecture on AWS
key_points: Medidata replaced many scheduled batch jobs, each building copies for a different consumer, with Flink streaming jobs on EKS that pass through MSK into Iceberg tables in the Glue Data Catalog.
One shared Iceberg copy serves all consumers; Glue's managed compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup handle table upkeep, and access is controlled centrally with IAM.
Short and high level, with no build details; AWS reports pipeline latency cut from hours or days to minutes.
services: Apache Iceberg, Apache Flink, Amazon EKS, Amazon MSK, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon S3
decision: Consumer-specific batch pipelines vs one streaming-fed shared Iceberg copy for many downstream consumers
authors: Medidata — Mike Araujo, Ashley Chen, Ian Beatty, Sandeep Adwankar

title: Introducing catalog federation for Apache Iceberg tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog
key_points: The Glue Data Catalog can now connect to remote Iceberg REST catalogs (Snowflake Polaris/Horizon, Databricks Unity, custom) and read their latest table metadata at query time instead of syncing it.
Lake Formation authorises access and hands engines short-lived credentials scoped to the table's S3 files, so Athena, EMR and Redshift query the remote tables with fine-grained permissions.
Launch post; the Jan 2026 Snowflake and Databricks walkthroughs and later customer stories cover it in practice.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, Amazon EMR
decision: Metadata sync jobs vs copying data vs catalog federation for querying Iceberg tables owned by another platform
authors: Debika D, Pratik Das, Srividya Parthasarathy

title: Getting started with Apache Iceberg write support in Amazon Redshift – Part 1
key_points: Redshift can now create Iceberg tables and INSERT into them, both in ordinary S3 buckets (via a Glue catalog external schema) and in S3 table buckets, with Lake Formation granting the S3 Tables permissions.
Tables written this way are immediately readable by Athena or EMR, and one Redshift query can join a plain-S3 Iceberg table with an S3 Tables one.
Part 1 covers creating and appending only; Parts 2 and 3 (2026) add row-level changes and table evolution, so the series works best as one hands-on write-up.

decision: Native Redshift tables vs Iceberg tables written from Redshift (S3 vs S3 Tables) for data other engines must also read

key_points: EMR 7.9's Spark runtime speeds up jobs that encrypt local shuffle and spill data, a setting regulated workloads often have to turn on.
AWS reports about 20% faster runtime and lower cost on a 3 TB TPC-DS run; a niche runtime note now covered by newer EMR releases.

title: Achieve 2x faster data lake query performance with Apache Iceberg on Amazon Redshift
key_points: Redshift Serverless got a rebuilt data lake scan layer for Parquet-based Iceberg tables, with prefetching and partition- and file-level pruning.

JIT ANALYZE samples Iceberg metadata at query time to give the planner statistics, so lake tables plan nearly as well as ones with collected stats; better subquery rewrites and distributed Bloom filters help large joins.
AWS reports over 2x faster TPC-DS and TPC-H runs on Iceberg during 2025, out of the box with no tuning.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless, Apache Iceberg
decision: Load lake data into Redshift managed storage vs query Iceberg in place from Redshift
authors: Kalaiselvi Kamaraj, Aamer Shah, Fabian Nagel, Ravi Animi, Stefan Gromoll

title: Accelerate data lake operations with Apache Iceberg V3 deletion vectors and row lineage
key_points: Iceberg V3 replaces piles of positional delete files with one compact deletion vector per data file, which cuts write amplification for frequent updates, CDC merges and GDPR deletes.

Row lineage adds a row id and last-updated sequence number to every row, so changed rows can be read incrementally without the V2 changelog's blind spot for rows inserted and deleted between snapshots.
Upgrading a V2 table is a metadata-only property change; check every engine that reads the table supports V3 first, and let managed compaction clean up old delete files.
services: Apache Iceberg, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Copy-on-write vs merge-on-read with V2 delete files vs V3 deletion vectors for update-heavy Iceberg tables
attaches_to: aws-bytes: File Layout Optimization (active); change data capture (later)
authors: Ron Ortloff

title: Save up to 24% on Amazon Redshift Serverless compute costs with Reservations
key_points: Redshift Serverless can now be reserved: commit to a number of RPUs for one year, billed around the clock, managed at the payer account and shared across linked accounts in the Region.

Size the commitment from the steady baseline, not the peak: the SYS_SERVERLESS_USAGE table and Cost Explorer recommendations show it; usage above the reservation is billed on demand and reservations cannot be reduced later.

AWS reports 20% off with no upfront and 24% all upfront; its worked examples show one spiky workgroup netting far less than the headline, while several workgroups pooling the reservation get the full discount.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless, AWS Billing and Cost Management
decision: Pure on-demand RPUs vs a reserved RPU baseline (no upfront vs all upfront) vs a provisioned cluster for steady Redshift Serverless use

key_points: Three-account setup: a producer account holds S3 Tables, a central governance account runs SageMaker Catalog, and a consumer account subscribes to assets and queries them with Athena.
Producers publish both S3 Tables and plain Glue catalog tables, consumers request access, and Lake Formation applies column-level grants once a request is approved.
Mostly console steps; useful mainly as a map of which account does what.

title: How Yelp modernized its data infrastructure with a streaming lakehouse on AWS
key_points: Yelp stopped using chains of Kafka topics as long-term storage: Flink on EKS with Flink CDC connectors writes into Apache Paimon tables on S3 that both streaming and batch SQL can query.
Moved from its in-house CDC format to standard Debezium, with a converter that kept old consumers working during the transition.

AWS reports analytics latency dropping from about 18 hours to minutes and storage cost down by over 80%; a useful example of the 'streamhouse' idea as an alternative to Iceberg for minute-level freshness.

title: Scaling data governance with Amazon DataZone: Covestro success story
key_points: Covestro split a central data lake into domain-owned data products: the Serverless Data Lake Framework deploys standard Glue ingestion and cleaning jobs from YAML, writing Iceberg tables with Glue Data Quality checks built in.
DataZone (now part of SageMaker Catalog) provides the shared catalog, glossary and access requests, with Lake Formation enforcing the grants across domains.
The most reusable idea is the cross-domain dependency check: a Step Functions step waits for upstream data products using central DynamoDB run logs, and a graph check catches circular dependencies.

title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams launches On-demand Advantage for instant throughput increases and streaming at scale
key_points: Launch of the account-level On-demand Advantage mode: no per-stream hourly fee and much cheaper throughput, in return for a minimum committed ingest and retrieval rate in the Region.
Warm throughput lets an on-demand stream be pre-sized for a known peak, so there is no more switching to provisioned mode and back before a big event.
AWS reports ingest and retrieval at least 60% cheaper; later posts (Mar and Sep 2026) give the fuller cost comparison and scale-down guidance, so this one is mainly background.
